text: You have n nodes labeled zero to n minus one, and a list of undirected edges. Return the number of connected components in the graph.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a connected component is a maximal group of nodes where every node is reachable from every other. And an isolated node with no edges counts as its own component. Is that right?

Let me run through an example. Five nodes, with edges zero-one, one-two, and three-four. Nodes zero, one and two are one blob, and three and four are another, so the answer is two. If there were no edges at all, every node would stand alone, and the answer would be five.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. This problem reminds me of flood fill on a graph, because counting components is just counting how many separate blobs there are. One way: DFS — build an adjacency list and loop over every node — each time I hit an unvisited one, that's a new component, so I bump the count and run a DFS to mark its whole blob. The other way is Union-Find: merge the two endpoints of every edge, then count how many roots remain. Both are close to linear. I'll show both; Union-Find is nicer if edges arrive online.

Here's the plan. One, for DFS: build the adjacency list in both directions, and start a count at zero. Two, for each node that is still unvisited, add one to the count and DFS from it. Three, for Union-Find: start every parent at negative one, union every edge, and count the entries that are still negative. One thing worth flagging — since the graph is undirected, I must push each edge both ways into the adjacency list; otherwise DFS can't always cross it and I'd over-count. And on the counting — in Union-Find every component has exactly one root, so counting negative parent entries gives the answer; equivalently, it's n minus the number of successful merges. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright — the DFS version first. It builds the adjacency list, then the outer loop skips visited nodes, and every node it doesn't skip adds one and starts a DFS that marks the whole blob. And the Union-Find version — same idea, counting roots instead. A negative parent means a root, and its absolute value is the size. Find compresses the path, and Union attaches the smaller tree under the larger one. One thing worth flagging — both loop the outer index over all n nodes, not just the ones touched by edges, so isolated nodes are counted correctly.

Let's dry-run both on five nodes, with edges zero-one, one-two, and three-four. In DFS, the count goes up only twice: at node zero, which marks zero, one and two, and at node three, which marks three and four. So it returns two. In Union-Find, after the three unions only nodes zero and three still have negative parents, so it also returns two. Corner case: with no edges, DFS starts a fresh blob at every index, and Union-Find leaves every parent at negative one, so both return n. Correct.

DFS is linear in time, V plus E, and its space is also V plus E, for the adjacency list plus the recursion stack. Union-Find takes V plus E times alpha of V, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function, so it's effectively linear — and its space is just V for the parent array. It never stores the graph. Oh, one more thing — if edges arrive one at a time and I need the running component count, Union-Find wins: keep a counter that starts at n and goes down by one on each successful merge. DFS would have to re-scan the whole graph each time.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You gave both approaches and mapped DFS launches and remaining roots to the same count. You flagged the both-ways adjacency for an undirected graph, a classic slip. And you handled isolated nodes by looping over every index. Good work.
